headline: Yellowfin fire at Hydrographer as bluefin migration finally kicks into gear
subhead: Eastern canyons come alive with late-season push as full moon tides trigger the bite
body_markdown:
The eastern canyons finally woke up this week, and it happened fast. After weeks of wondering where the hell everything went, Hydrographer Canyon exploded with yellowfin action that had boats scrambling to get out there before the weather window closed.

The yellowfin bite at Hydrographer has been nothing short of spectacular. We're talking 40- to 80-pound fish coming up from 200 to 300 feet, hitting spreads of cedar plugs and daisy chains like they haven't eaten in weeks. The key has been working the 100-fathom curve where the canyon wall drops off — that's where the thermocline is setting up and stacking bait. Green machines and pink Ilanders in the short riggers, with a couple of ballyhoo way back in the long corner have been the ticket. Don't overthink it — these fish are aggressive and hungry.

What's really got me excited is the bluefin situation. After running two to three weeks behind schedule all season, the big fish finally showed up in numbers off Block Island and the Race. We're seeing 200- to 400-pound fish mixed in with the school bluefin, and they're not just passing through — they're feeding. The full moon tides this week pushed massive amounts of bunker and sand eels out of the Sound, and the bluefin followed the feed right to our doorstep.

The white marlin have been a bonus in the spread while targeting the yellowfin. Nothing huge — most are running 50 to 70 pounds — but they're there, and they're eating the same baits. Circle hooks on the ballyhoo have been crucial for the clean releases, and the fish have been coming up healthy and strong.

Mahi have been scattered but consistent in the 68- to 70-degree water. The bigger fish — bulls pushing 30 pounds — have been holding around floating debris and weed lines about 15 miles southeast of the main canyon structure. Small feathers and spoons trolled at 8 knots have been producing, but you need to cover water to find them.

The real story this week has been water temperature and structure. The eastern canyons are holding that magic 68- to 72-degree water while the inshore stuff is still running cool. That temperature break is everything — it's where the bait concentrates and where the pelagics set up to feed. Veatch Canyon has been producing similar action, though the yellowfin there have been running smaller, mostly in the 30- to 50-pound class.

Timing has been critical. The full moon tides are moving fast — really fast — and that's triggering aggressive feeding behavior. We've been getting out there for the dawn bite, working spreads at 7 to 8 knots, and staying flexible. When the fish are up, they're really up. When they're down, you need to get the jigs and poppers ready and work the water column.

The late start to the season means we're compressed into a shorter window, but the quality is there. These aren't the usual June fish — they're thick, healthy, and feeding hard. The bluefin quota situation is interesting too. We're way under the numbers they projected for this time of year, which means there's still plenty of opportunity for the boats willing to make the run.

Looking ahead, the weather pattern is setting up for another good stretch. Southwest winds through the weekend should keep the eastern canyons fishable, and the new moon next week could really light things up. The bait is thick, the water temperature is right, and the fish are finally here in numbers. This is what we've been waiting for all season — don't let it pass you by.
